n: Joseph sets a final test. He orders their sacks filled with all they can carry and their money returned again.
He has his personal silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack. The test: will the brothers abandon Rachel’s other son to slavery, as they once abandoned Joseph?
At first light the brothers departed, relieved and happy, with Simeon and Benjamin safe.
Not long after, Joseph sent his steward after them to accuse them of repaying kindness with theft.

f.w: Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good?
f.g: Why have you repaid good with evil?

n: The steward claims it is the cup Joseph uses for divination—a part of Joseph’s Egyptian disguise. It does not mean Joseph actually practiced fortune-telling.

f.g: practices divination; ancient diviners read signs in liquid poured into a cup

n: The steward catches up and delivers the accusation word for word.
The brothers are shocked and deny it: “God forbid” they would do such a thing.
They argue sensibly: we brought back money we didn’t owe—why would we steal silver or gold?
So sure of their innocence, they make a rash vow: let the guilty one die and the rest become slaves—echoing Jacob’s rash words when Laban searched for his idols.
The steward softens the terms: only the guilty one will become a slave; the rest may go free. This makes the test sharper—the others can simply walk away.
Each brother quickly unloaded and opened his sack.
The search went oldest to youngest, building suspense, and the cup was found in Benjamin’s sack.
In grief the brothers tore their clothes. But they did not abandon Benjamin—every one of them reloaded and returned to the city with him. This is the change Joseph hoped to see.
Judah—named first now as the leader—and his brothers fell on the ground before Joseph.
Joseph demands an explanation, keeping up his Egyptian role.
Judah does not argue. He confesses that “God hath found out” their iniquity—likely thinking of their old sin against Joseph—and offers all of them as slaves.

f.w: God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants

n: Joseph refuses: only Benjamin will stay; the rest can go home “in peace.” This is the decisive moment of the test.
Judah steps forward to plead. What follows is one of the most moving speeches in Genesis.

f.g: you have authority equal to Pharaoh’s

n: Judah begins by recounting how the lord had asked about their family.
He explains that their elderly father dearly loves this youngest son, the only remaining son of his mother. Judah now speaks of Jacob’s favoritism without bitterness.

f.w: a child of his old age

n: Judah recalls the lord’s demand to see the youngest brother.
They had warned that taking Benjamin might kill their father.
But the lord insisted they must bring him or not return.
Judah reports telling their father everything.
Their father had asked them to go buy food again.
They explained they could not go without Benjamin.
Judah quotes Jacob: my wife bore me two sons. Jacob’s words show his love was centered on Rachel—yet Judah repeats them with compassion, not resentment.
Jacob had concluded one son was torn to pieces. Judah, who knew the truth, carried this lie in his heart.

f.w: Surely he is torn in pieces

n: Judah repeats his father’s fear that losing Benjamin would kill him with grief.

f.w: bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave

n: Their father’s life is “bound up” in the boy’s life—so tightly knit that losing one would destroy the other.

f.w: his life is bound up in the lad's life

n: If Judah returns without Benjamin, his father will die, and the brothers will be to blame.
Judah explains that he personally pledged himself for Benjamin’s safety.

Judah offers to become a slave in Benjamin’s place. The man who once sold his brother now gives himself for his brother—a powerful picture of repentance and a type of Christ, the descendant of Judah who took our place.

f.w: let thy servant abide instead of the lad

n: Judah cannot bear to see his father’s grief. His love for Jacob and Benjamin is now greater than his self-interest—exactly the change Joseph needed to see.
